fr:mainmatter.html:p: Models of geolog theories are stored as collections of tables. For the reader experienced with traditional relational databases, tables should be fairly familiar, but we will go through them explicitly in order to establish our own conventions.
A table consists of a set of row IDs and a collection of columns. A table may come along with constraints, and in particular primary key constraints

Row IDs are an opaque type to the user, kind of like pointers without pointer arithmetic. In particular, a row ID may be dereferenced to look up the corresponding row in the database, and row IDs may be stored in columns to link tables together, but the content of a row ID is not meant to be meaningful or even stable.

This is becasue row IDs may exist in different formats in-memory, on disk, and over the network, and moreover may be subject to garbage-collection-like algorithms periodically in order to improve storage properties of the database.

A column is a sequence of values of some fixed data type, like String, Bool, Int, or RowId. Columns store one value for each row ID of the table they belong to, and they store these values in such a way so that it is efficient to access the corresponding value for each row ID. This could be achieved by storing the row IDs in sorted order, and storing the values in each column in the same order, so that a binary search over row IDs would produce the right index to access the column value at, but it is also possible that row IDs take the values 0,\ldots ,n-1, and columns may be directly indexed by row ID; the choice of how precisely this achieved is not something that is relevant at this level of abstraction.

As users do not interact with columns directly, we can identify the columns in a table by a simple sequential numbering 0,\ldots ,k-1; we call the number assigned to a column in this fashion its column index.

A primary key constraint is specified by a subset K \subseteq \{0,\ldots ,k-1\} of column indices. For each K-indexed tuple of values, a table satisfying the primary key constraint may have at most one row with columns assigned as in that K-tuple.

This can be used in a variety of ways. If K = \{0,\ldots ,k-1\}, then the table is a proper relation. If K = \{0,\ldots ,\ell -1\}, then K is a partial function from the first \ell column values to the last k - \ell column values.
A table with no primary key constraint can be thought of as a bag.
As a degenerate case, a table with no columns and a primary key constraint of \{\} has either zero or one row IDs.

Tables also have associated constraints. We discuss these in greater detail once we talk about how geolog theories are lowered to a collection of tables; essentially the constraints are what enforces the type dependencies between the different arguments to a function.
Geolog can work as a little proof assistant which is restricted to positive types, but the real point of this restriction is to enable a translation to the database world.
One could look at this in two ways, depending on whether you think of the language or the database as “primary.”

In one sense, because the database engine can be used to reason about models defined purely in geolog, the database engine is essentially a souped-up tactic (in the sense of Rocq or Lean) for enumerating the elements of types.

But not all models of geolog theories need to be defined in geolog itself. As we have seen, the automatically-produced TypeScript functions can be used to initialize and populate a model in an imperative style. For instance, when using geolog to do an egglog-style analysis of a C-like language, one would first write a parser and type checker in a normal programming language, and then issue mutations via the API to create a model that represented the IR of the program. Then geolog queries could be run against that IR to resolve questions about the behavior of the program.
Thus, geolog is not a typical proof assistant; geolog is a tool that is meant to be integrated into a larger program that is not written in geolog.

In order to give the programmer a mental model for how they can expect these commands to work, in this section of the manual we describe the translation from a theory in the geolog language to a collection of tables.

The key idea in translating a geolog theory into a usable database schema is that we can distribute records over functions. To understand this idea, first consider geolog theories of a special form.
A theory is in \Sigma \Pi normal form if a record type never appears in the codomain of a function type.

fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory Graph := sig vertex : Set edge : vertex -> vertex -> Set end

fr:title.text: Bag of graphs is not in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Bag of graphs is not in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:mainmatter.html:pre: theory BagOfGraphs := sig graph-id : Set graph-for : graph-id -> Graph end
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Because Graph is a record type and it appears in the codomain of graph-for, BagOfGraphs is not in \Sigma \Pi normal form.

If a theory is in \Sigma \Pi normal form, it is fairly straightforward to represent it as a collection of tables. Specifically, ignoring the type dependency for now, each function type is of the form A1 -> A2 -> ... -> AN -> B, where A1,...,AN are all sets, and B is either a set, Set, or Prop. Then

html:ul.html:li: If B is a set, then we can represent this as a table with columns A1,...,AN,B and a primary key constraint on A1,...,AN.
If B is Set, then this is a table with columns A1,...,AN and no primary key constraint.
If B is Prop, then this is a table with columns A1,...,AN and a primary key constraint on A1,...,AN.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Thus, the first job to do when translating a geolog theory into a database schema is to put the geolog theory in \Sigma \Pi normal form.

fr:title.text: Bag of graphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Bag of graphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We can put BagOfGraphs in \Sigma \Pi normal form and then convert back and forth between the normal and original representations in the following way.
fr:mainmatter.html:pre:
theory BagOfGraphs/normal := sig graph-id : Set graph-for/vertex : graph-id -> Set graph-for/edge : (i : graph-id) -> graph-for/vertex i -> graph-for/vertex i -> Set end
def from-normal (m : BagOfGraphs/normal) : BagOfGraphs := struct graph-id := m.graph-id graph-for := i => struct vertex := m.graph-for/vertex i edge := v0 => v1 => m.graph-for/edge i v0 v1 end end
def to-normal (m : BagOfGraphs) : BagOfGraphs/normal := struct graph-id := m.graph-id graph-for/vertex := i => m.graph-for i .vertex graph-for/edge := i => v0 => v1 => m.graph-for i .edge v0 v1 end

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In this way, although when writing down BagOfGraphs it appears as if we would store a separate graph database for each graph id, in fact all of the graphs are stored in the same pair of tables. In particular, allocating a new graph id does not imply allocating a whole new graph structure.

There is a fairly straightforward algorithm to take a general theory to a theory in \Sigma \Pi -normal form, producing the from-normal and to-normal migrations simultaneously, but describing it here would involve a conceptual framework around the elaborator which would take a while to get off the ground. Thus, we ask the reader to take as given that we have access to such an algorithm, and we continue on assuming that we are working with theories in \Sigma \Pi -normal form.
One way of thinking about this algorithm is that it is a generalized version of the array-of-structs to struct-of-arrays transformation in, for instance, Zig's MultiArrayList.
